content: 1. When caring for patients with suspected or confirmed Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) or Marburg Virus Disease (MVD), and maintaining a distance of at least 1 meter from the patient is not feasible, it is recommended to use two pairs of gloves for added protection. 2. Research is required to evaluate the effectiveness of various personal protective equipment (PPE) elements, both individually and as a complete ensemble, through simulation studies to determine optimal choices. 3. PPE designs should be tailored to accommodate the anatomical and hygiene needs of both men and women, including considerations for menstrual hygiene management for female healthcare workers. 4. The recommended PPE for healthcare workers providing direct or indirect care to patients with suspected or confirmed EVD or MVD includes the following: Scrubs Closed-toe shoes Two pairs of nitrile gloves A medical mask combined with eye protection (either a face shield or goggles) A coverall Head and neck covering (with eye protection worn underneath) A disposable or reusable apron 5. PPE must completely cover the mucous membranes of the eyes, mouth, and nose to prevent exposure to infectious agents. This recommendation is based on high-certainty evidence and is critical for infection prevention. 6. When removing PPE, items protecting the mucous membranes should be taken off last to minimize the risk of accidental exposure to contaminated surfaces. 7. Reusable goggles or face shields must undergo proper decontamination procedures to ensure safety. 8. Training healthcare workers in the correct use and sizing of PPE is essential, along with ensuring a continuous supply of PPE items and establishing protocols for reuse or disposal as appropriate. 9. Protection of the mucous membranes of the eyes, nose, and mouth is a fundamental component of standard and droplet precautions, as contamination of these areas is a primary mode of filovirus transmission. 10. Goggles should provide a good seal with the skin, fit comfortably without excessive pressure, and allow for panoramic vision. They should also be fogand scratch-resistant, adjustable, and, if reusable, capable of being decontaminated. 11. Face shields should be made of clear plastic, provide full coverage of the face, and be fog-resistant. They should fit snugly against the forehead and be either reusable (with proper cleaning and disinfection) or disposable. 12. There is no comparative evidence on the effectiveness of face shields versus goggles for preventing filovirus transmission. However, face shields are often preferred due to better visibility, comfort, and reduced fogging. 13. Goggles are associated with more discomfort, fogging, and interference with vision and communication compared to face shields. These issues can compromise patient care and increase the risk of accidental exposure. 14. Surgical masks are generally preferred over particulate respirators (e.g., N95) due to greater comfort and usability, though they provide limited protection during aerosol-generating procedures. 15. Particulate respirators, while offering higher protection, are associated with increased discomfort, heat stress, and communication difficulties, which can impact the well-being and performance of healthcare workers. 16. The choice between face shields and goggles, as well as between surgical masks and respirators, should consider personal preferences, local availability, and technical specifications, ensuring that the selected PPE meets safety and comfort requirements. 17. Anti-fogging products, such as sprays, may help reduce fogging in goggles, but their effectiveness may vary in hot and humid climates. 18. Training materials and protocols for the safe disposal or decontamination of PPE should be developed to support healthcare workers in their use of protective equipment. 19. The biology and transmission mode of the Ebola virus informed the development of technical specifications for PPE, emphasizing the importance of structured designs for masks to prevent collapse against the face and ensure adequate protection.
